p: Right.

You know, as we know, medical debt is the biggest driver of personal bankruptcy in the city for New Yorkers. And the work that we’ve done has been a tremendous start. We’ve been able to erase about $135 million in medical debt so far. Just over half of the individuals who have received those envelopes in the mail, relieving them of their debt are in tree neighborhoods. And so, you know, we see this as an incredibly important tool in our tool kit when it comes to addressing health care

affordability. With regard to the future of the program, yeah, we’re working very close with Undue Medical Debt to identify how we can leverage that $18 million and really make sure that we make a dent on that issue. And so, you know, the conversations are ongoing and this is a personal place of personal interest of mine.

Thank you. And just out of curiosity, how are communities and individuals identified for inclusion in the program as a, you know, first step, and then are there geographic or income-based targeting criteria. And then the second part of my question which is not in here which is something close to me is how are those people being reached out to? Because I know you said mail. But in different languages? Because as we know, we’re a very diverse city, and some folks may look at it. If it’s English, they might just discard it and not realize. So, just wondering what the outreach efforts are as well, once those folks are identified?

Yeah. it’s a really good question. So, first of all, we are working to cancel debt citywide. Now, the

individuals who do receive the interventions typically end up being from communities that have rates of– legacies of historic disinvestment. As I mentioned, over 50 percent of those who have received intervention are in those tree neighborhoods. And so there is targeting to make sure that we are helping folks who are low-income, communities of color, individuals who are underinsured, uninsured, and we’re building that sort of broader monitoring infrastructure to make sure that we can really target this intervention.
Great. And then I guess roughly in your estimates, how much support would that amount to dollar-wise as well?

It’s a great question. You know, we, Chair, are taking advantage of the ability to buy debt cheaply here, and so that $18 million, if we add that up, you know, as we think about how we can go on the market and buy that debt from participating hospitals, we can get into the billions. You know, the numbers range between $1.5 and $2 billion, and so you know, we’re aiming to hit those targets. And I’ll say one other piece and that

is that the issue of medical debt can be addressed in different ways. And so we are looking at all the different levers that are possible, and this partnership with Undue [sic] is essential part of that plan.
Okay, great. And how much of that $18 million invested is reflected in the budget for DOHMH?
That’s a good question. Let me hand it over to Aaron Anderson to shed a little more on that.
Yeah, so it’s $6 million per year. So, there’s $6 million included in FY27.
Okay, perfect. And I think I know the answer to this, but is the allocation sufficient to meet the $2 billion relief goal?

You know, so the goal of this work is to really work closely with Undue Medical Debt to make sure that that funding that we have can be used as effectively and as efficient as possible. And so we’re working closely

with them to try and identify how to do that, how to maximize the money that we have.

Okay. Thank you so much. And that’s why I just want to reiterate definitely and issue in terms of communities of color, for sure where it negatively impacts them a great deal, and this is why prevention is so important. Because we need to make sure that we’re keeping people healthy which saves the city and state dollars in the long run. So, thank you so much for your work, and that’s it. Thank you, Chair.
Thanks, Chair.

Thank you, Chair. So, I also want to be– I’m going to ask somebody, one of my colleagues to ask questions so that they can move on to their next hearing. But I also want to mention in terms of Undue Medical Debt that the CEO of Undue Medical Debt is a friend and constituent of mine, so and she’s– her program is being done across the country. She’s met with the governors of almost every state. So, I’m very glad that we’re doing work with her and that we can relieve people of their medical debt which I think the President just said

that they’re not going to let people take that off of their credit reports anymore. So, that’s– so it’s even more needed. I’m going to ask Council Member Ossé to ask some questions, and then I’ll get to mine. COUNCIL MEMBER OSSÉ: Thank you so much, Chair, and congratulations and welcome to the new Commissioner. My constituents are concerned about the closure of the Crown Heights Clinic. This clinic provided a variety of key health care services to my constituents that they truly depended on, including rapid COVID, Flu, RSV rapid testing, as well as STI testing. Constituents are concerned that with the closure of this clinic, many will lose access to accessible rapid testing, especially those with chronic illnesses who need to know their COVID status sooner rather than later to ensure they can get Paxlovid or other COVID prevention treatment on time. My first question is why did the Department of Health decide to close down this clinic? And I know that this took place prior to you being in this position, but many are requesting this question from my office.

Yeah. First of all, thank you for your leadership on this issue, Council Member. As you know, we offer a range of clinics which are low-cost to no-cost clinics. We have six sexual health clinics, three TB chest centers, and then one immunization clinic, and what we see coming through these clinics is because we’re providing low barrier of care services for folks, we see that about 87 percent of the individuals that are coming in are historically disenfranchised with regard to the clinics that have been closed. Three of those clinics were closed during COVID. So, we have, you know, a priority around trying to reopen the Washington Heights and the Crown Heights clinic which you mentioned. And so, that is absolutely a priority of ours. At present moment we don’t have the ability to do that, but we are absolutely intending to move in that direction. COUNCIL MEMBER OSSÉ: So, you said– I really do appreciate that there is a plan to reopen those clinics. What are the obstacles in getting to the reopening of this specific clinic?
Yeah. Let me clarify. We certainly are interested in doing so. COUNCIL MEMBER OSSÉ: Sure.

And the ability to do so is going to be contingent on the funding and the resources to be able to do that. And so we’re in constant conversations with our colleagues at OMB and across City Hall to do this, and we look forward to working with you and continue that conversation around what the future holds. COUNCIL MEMBER OSSÉ: Do you have any idea in terms of how much it would cost to open one of these clinics? Like, if I were to advocate for the reopening of this specific Crown Heights clinic, how much should I be advocating to the mayor to include within the budget?
Yeah. Good question. Let me hand it over to Aaron.

Thanks for the question. We’re actively working on estimates and potential projections and continuing those conversations with OMB. So, there’s not a specific number at this time.

COUNCIL MEMBER OSSÉ: Okay. I appreciate hearing that. Another– may I ask one more question? My constituents are also concerned about the lack of gender-affirming care in the city. We’re also aware of NYC Langone’s decision to close its trangender youth health program. As the federal administration continues to threaten health care facilities and roll back funding from LGBTQ+ health organizations, as I’m sure you know, health care that is accessible and safe for queer and trans New Yorkers is now a pressing issue for our city. How can the Department of Health ensure that gender affirming care services and other health resources for LGBTQ+ New Yorkers continue to remain available in H+H clinics, and the other DOHMH sites?

Thank you again for your leadership on this issue, counselor. We are very much invested in the care for individuals in the trans community and non-binary community, and think it’s a priority of ours to make sure that we can provide the services that this community needs. We recently met with the Commissioner on Gender Equity to begin really thinking through how we can do a

better job prioritizing the needs of this community, but this is something that we’ll continue pressing on, you know, working with you and your team on making sure this is reality. COUNCIL MEMBER OSSÉ: Sure. love to hear from both of you especially when it comes to budgetary costs of how much of these issues would cost, right? I think it would help on our side of things being able to advocate for this funding. So, whenever you do have those numbers, I would love to hear back from your office. Thank you, Chair.
We can follow up.

Thank you. I just want to acknowledge we’ve been joined by Council Member Nurse. So, now we’ll have– I have a bunch of questions for you, Commissioner. In the Preliminary Plan, DOHMH has federal funding decreased by $32.8 million in Fiscal 2027, compared to the Fiscal 2026 Adopted Budget. The city primarily receives federal funding for the disease prevention and treatment program area in which communicable diseases had the highest decrease in funding, followed by sexually transmitted infections and tuberculosis. We remain

concerned that the city might lose part or even all its federal dollars for health services. Is the reduction of $32.8 million due to the federal government’s new policies or is it due to external factors?

Yeah, thank you for that question, Chair. You know, we share your concern with what we’re seeing at the federal government and the way they’ve threatened public health funding, the way that they’re communicating with regard to public health messaging. You know, we are in an unprecedented era here. And also, we are not going to wait for the federal government to come in, swoop in and save us here in the city. We are leading. We are stepping in and we are making sure that New Yorkers have what they need to be safe and healthy. With regard to the $32.8 million that you discussed. That reduction is actually not due to the federal government clawing back funding. That’s due to the fact that these federal grants have not fully been loaded yet in the Preliminary Budget, and so we think that once those are loaded, the expected federal funds will be about 20 percent of our total

budget or around $500 million a year. And that’s sort of the standard budget timing, and these are not confirmed cuts.
Okay.

And Chair Schulman, I’m sorry. Just to add to that, it’s true a lot of our funding, as you acknowledged in the opening is loaded over time with one exception. So, it’s not a cut, but there is the expiration of federal COVID funding, supplemental funding. That’s ending this July. And so actually when we sat here, this hearing last year exactly one year ago and said that $100 million was what we had left, the day after that hearing it was rescinded and replaced. But we’re basically in the final stages of spending that last amount down.
So, that’ll be– that’ll be how much less for next fiscal year?
So, the final amount currently of that supplemental funding is about $32-$35 million. So, that’s–
[interposing] Okay.
one of the reasons that’s contributing here.
Alright. What are the major federal grants that DOHMH received for health care in fiscal year 2026?

Thank you for that question, Chair. In FY 2026 we received $453 million in federal funding. More than half of that supports disease control. We’re talking about surveillance, labs, HIV support, childhood vaccinations. Just double-clicking on the HIV and STI funding which is about $225 million, 87 percent of that budget comes from federal funding sources. I’ll hand it over to Aaron to share anything else he’s got.

Yeah, thanks for the question. So, some of the major federal grants that we receive include Ryan White which is probably the biggest, epidemiology and laboratory capacity, housing opportunity for people’s with AIDS which we split with the Department of Social Services, public health emergency preparedness, and then we have our core cooperative awards for TB control and immunization. Those are

sort of the biggest ticket pieces of our federal portfolio.
Right. Yeah. Has– have you– for Fiscal 2026, has DOHMH received reimbursement for all its programs as anticipated? It sounds like.
Yeah, we have not experienced any significant changes this year and we remain–
[interposing] And do you expect any of the federal grants to be reduced or eliminated. I mean, I know it goes back and forth, but–

I mean, based on our best reading of the tea leaves and the budget that the feds passed, the continuing resolution, it appears to be okay at the moment, but we’ve certainly experienced whiplash over the past year, but we’re in an okay place right now.
Excluding any COVID-19-related funding which you just mentioned, how much funding do you anticipate that DOHMH will receive from the federal government by adoption?
So, we expect the total to be around $500 million, around 20 percent of our budget. It’s hard to know exactly until then.
Okay, alright. Does DOHMH have a contingency plan if the federal government withholds funding?

Yeah, thank you for that, Chair Schulman. We are closely monitoring the situation. We’re trying to really, as Aaron said, read the tea leaves and predict what might be coming down the path, but we are currently in active discussion with OMB, with the Law Department and the Mayor’s Office to come up with plans. If there are cuts to specific activities, we will assess and make decision around what will protect New Yorker’s health and safety the best in those moments.

Okay. the New York State Fiscal 2027 Executive Budget proposed total spending of $260 billion compared to $252 billion in Fiscal 2026. Within the city’s budget, DOHMH’s Fiscal 2027 Preliminary Budget includes $311.5 million in state funding for health services,

an increase of nearly $65 million compared to last year’s adopted budget. How much funding do you anticipate DOHMH will receive from New York State Fiscal 2027 enacted budget for public health programs?

Thank you for that question, Chair. As you know, the funding that comes into this department is really broken up in three different sections, City Tax Levy, the feds, and the state. And so we work very closely with our state colleagues and we’re encouraged by what we’re seeing in the Governor’s commitment to restoring critical public health. We’re going to talk about Article 6 in a bit, but you know, what we’re seeing in the FY 27 state funds is that the funding that we’ll get from the state is about $722 million which represents approximately 30 percent of our total budget. I’m going to hand it over to Aaron to share more.

Yeah, thanks, Commissioner. Right. So, that’s the total state amount for the entire Department. On the public health side alone, we’re expecting probably around the order of $400 million, and a big piece of

that is of course the Article 6 restoration which we’re delighted to have.
Which DOHMH programs are expected to receive the largest share of state funding?
I’m going to hand it to you, Aaron.
Thanks. The single largest program on the state side is early intervention.

Okay, that’s great. The state’s Medicaid program serves 6.8 million New Yorkers and the Executive Budget includes changes to the essential plan and Medicaid eligibility due to federal policy changes and funding reductions under HR1. How will the proposed transition from the Section 1332 waiver back to the basic health program under Section 1331 impact New York residents, particularly the more than 460,000 essential plane enrollees expected to lose coverage when the income eligibility threshold is reduced from 250 and 200 percent of the federal poverty level?

Yeah, thank you for that question. We share your concern, Chair. The transition from Section 1332 to 1331 is– put simply going to mean that more people will lose their health coverage. And as we know, 460,000 of those folks who will likely be affected by this change, the majority of those people are here in this city.
Right.

And so, the ultimate estimates around DOH at the state is thinking about is about 713,000 New Yorkers will potentially lose their coverage through a combination of all of these different federal policy changes. And so we have not remained stagnant on this. We are not sitting back. We’ve submitted, you know, public comment to limit the essential impact, essential plan impact. We’re planning public education, provider outreach, advocacy, to try to meet the moment and help keep people covered.

Yeah, I mean, it’s interesting because none of this was in any of the one state assembly or senate, their budgets that they put out. So, which was to be, but okay. So, we have

to keep advocating for that. Federal changes will eliminate eligibility for certain non-citizens populations and federal medicaid support for some legally present immigrants beginning in October of 2026. How many New York City residents could be affected and what steps are being taken to ensure they maintain access to coverage.

Yeah. Thank you for that question, Chair. We are, again, alarmed. We share your concern with what the federal administration is doing. In effect, they are abusing immigration law in ways that are dangerous to resident’s health, to their wellbeing. And this is going to quite frankly going to mean that not only will there be a chilling effect across, you know, individuals coming to our sites, but also health care sites throughout the city, and then on top of that you add the fact that coverage will also be threatened for these communities. And so, what we are doing– we launched the Every New Yorker without Exception campaign and adopted policies restricting cooperation with ICE on DOHMH property, but we know the fight is not over. We know we have to continue

to push and to advocate and to make sure that we protect folks in the city.
But how many New York City residents you think could be affected by those changes?
The state estimates that we have from New York State is in total about 713,000 New Yorkers.
That’s for the state, right?
for the state, yah.
What about the city?
We can get back to you in terms of, you know, sort of the slice of that are city and the slice that are–

[interposing] Would like to have that. Aaron, you don’t have those figures? Okay, alright. The Executive Budget notes that federal policy changes will significantly reduce federal funding for the Essential Plan or the health services. What fiscal and coverage impact could

these changes have on New York City residents and the providers– and the providers that serve them?

Yeah. I mean, the overall impact here, Chair, is that we’re going to likely see an increase in uncompensated care. You know folks are not going to be covered, because not only did– not only will we see the changes which will hit in July to essential and basic plan, but we’re also going to see these new changes which will hit in January of 2027 around Medicaid specifically. But we also have to acknowledge what happened in December of 2025 wich congress’ failure to sustain the ACA subsidies which has meant that premiums have increased by quite a bit, 38 percent.
Right.

So we have a number of different things that are happening here which are leading to individuals not being covered. So we think that ultimately we’re going to have more individuals who are going to likely need uncompensated care going to places like H+H, our partners across the city and other safety net

providers, and we are helping New Yorkers explore alternative coverage and affordable care options.
What coordination is occurring between the state and city to prepare providers and enrollees for these policy changes?

So, you know, I can speak, you know, from the perspective of the Health Department. We are committed to using every single lever we have to help individuals stay covered, to know that they have to do these work requirements which now have to happen every single month, helping them do their renewals which now will have to happen twice a year. And so we’re committed to trying to find every single intervention we can do to that work.

In New York State, total medicaid and essential plan spending is projected to reach $122.9 billion in fiscal 2027, including $65 billion in federal funding and $48.5 billion in state funding. In Fiscal 2027, the state will also assume nearly $9.2 billion in costs that could have otherwise had been incurred by localities. How much Medicaid funding does DOHMH currently

receive, and how might that change in the Fiscal 2027 Executive State Budget?

Yeah, thank you for that question, Chair. Medicaid is a critical funding source for so much of the core programs that allow New Yorkers in this city to get the care they need. And so we have a number of Medicaid-dependent programs, our early intervention program, our mental hygiene contracted services like supportive housing, ACT team, IMT team, and our public health clinics. And so we’re working with our colleagues at OMB to really assess the full exposure and what might be coming down the pike here. So, let me hand it over to Aaron to see if he has something else to add.
Sure. Just to add to that, so we receive approximately $68 million–
[interposing] Okay.

in Medicaid funding. And that’s a combination. It’s really two parts. There’s the direct services we get reimbursed for, and then there’s Medicaid admin. So, depending on the programs, it’s one of those two

things. But we do expect a similar amount for the next year.
Which DOHMH programs rely most heavily on that Medicaid funding?

I can share and then have Aaron add on. So, as I mentioned a couple of the programs that rely very heavily are early intervention. And so that is very much part of– Medicaid is very much a part of the revenue that we rely on for patients to get the care, New Yorkers to get the care they need through the eraly intervention program, our sexual health clinics, TB chest centers, school-based health centers, and the mental hygiene contracted services. So, all of these different programs serve Medicaid-enrolled individuals. Let me hand it over to–

[interposing] Can you get us what– you may not have it now– what percentage of those program budgets are supported by Medicaid, a breakdown. Alright, if you can get that to us, that would be great. Because like I said, we want to advocate, so we want to figure this out. The state budget provides an additional $75 million for

the medical indemnity fund in addition to it’s $52 million base. How many New York City are currently supported through the indemnity fund?

Yeah, thank you for that. We’re committed to ensuring that children with birth-related neurological injuries receive all the support that they need. As you know, the medical indemnity fund is state administered program, and so we’re working to support that, support the state in their efforts, but we don’t directly manage enrollment or distribute those funds.
Okay.
Let me hand it over to Aaron to see if there’s anything else to add.
Yeah, just to add that as with so many of these state initiatives, we’re closely monitoring what’s going on with the state budget, and you know, we’ll see what’s agreed to in the Executive Budget.
Right.
And the enacted budget in April, and take it from there.
With what’s been stated as potential additional funding, will that expand coverage for New York City children? We don’t know yet, right?
Which additional funding?

The state budget is giving $75 million more for the fund. We don’t know, okay. Article 6 which I took on as soon as I took office in 2022 and we’ve been advocating ever since and then was joined last year by Assemblymember Gonzalez-Rojas and State Senator Gustavo Rivera, and we were finally able to get that done, and I’m very appreciative of that, and we’ve been pushing. It’s been on the agenda, with the council’s agenda, with the state for all those years, and I had the privilege this past weekend to meet with the Governor and thank her personally for that. So, I’m very happy that we have that. So, with that additional restoration of $60 million for Fiscal 2027, what programs and services are going to be– are we going to be able to restore funding to or what programs and services will be supported with that $60 million?
Yeah. First, before I answer that, just to say thank you for your leadership and for your advocacy on that issue. This is a hugely important equity issue as you know.
Yep.
You know, that disproportionate share of individuals who are on Medicaid are here in the city, so we need every single dollar in the city to–
[interposing] Right.
be able to carry out the core public health mission of the work. I’m going to hand it over to Aaron to talk a little bit about the specifics of how the money’s flowing.
Did we get that yet, or we didn’t? We’re going to get it when the budget passes, is that the way it–
[interposing] We’re optimistic and confident that it will appear in the final budget. It’s in the initial budget. So, it’s–
[interposing] Well, if it doesn’t, you tell– we’ll figure it out. But–
[interposing] Yeah, and just echoing the Commissioner’s thank you to the rest of the council.
Yeah.
So, this sort of reverses a major cost-shift from the state to the city that occurred under prior admins dating back to 2019.
Yeah.
The biggest change now is that we will no longer need to cover with city funds the difference between the 20 percent reimbursement–
[interposing] Right. That was the issue.

which is what it was and now it’s 36 percent. So, it’s really– this is about core public health services. It’s family health. It’s communicable disease control, it’s chronic disease prevention. It’s environmental health, emergency response and then it

goes on and on. So, this is a huge change, and it’s really reversing this cost shift that had been in place for so many years.
We should– when we get that money, maybe we should do something publicly around what we’re going to be funding so that they–
[interposing] Love that.

so the state can see what the– the Governor can see firsthand like what we did. Maybe invite her or something. If Article– let’s see. Do you anticipate that a full restoration of Article 6 funding would allow the city to reinvest local dollars into other public health priorities?

You know, Chair, we think that a full restoration would certainly free up additional city resources. And so with those extra resources, you know, I think the core public health functions of the Department and all of the contracted CBOs that we work with will be made more effective and reach more people.

Okay, the– by the way, I want to acknowledge we’ve been joined by Majority Leader Shaun Abreu. The Mayor’s Preliminary– Mayor’s Management Report metrics indicates that 1,791 people were newly diagnosed with HIV in calendar year 2024, up from 1,700 in 2023, 1,591 in 2022. This marks the second consecutive annual increase following a decade of steady declines prior to 2020. The PMMR also notes persistent inequities with the majority of new diagnoses among Black and Latino New Yorkers, men and people ages 20 to 39. At the same time, 90 percent of people with HIV or in care have achieved viral suppression. What factors may be contributing to the recent increase in new HIV diagnoses?

Thank you for that question, Chair. So, we use a multipronged approach to improving access to testing, to treatment, and to prevention. This is a complicated question in terms of what’s driving these rates, but some of the factors include things like increased testing engagement, population changes, possible increased transmission, but also some of the structural more

difficult social determinants of health issues, poverty, housing stability, lack of insurance, and unmet service needs. And so, we know that this is an area that we need to watch closely to make sure that these trends don’t continue, and we’re committed to investing every single resource we can to reversing that trend.
What outreach and testing strategies is DOHMH using to reach communities most affected by HIV, particularly Black and Latino New Yorkers?

Thank you. I’ll say a few words, and then I would love to Dr. Braunstein join me. But we have a number of sexual health clinics that we currently operate, six sexual health clinics, a tele-health hotline, the Play Sure [sic] Network 2.0, one-stop model, our considerable resources around Ryan White, and so we have a number of tools at our disposal to really tackle this problem head-on, but let me hand it over to Dr. Braunstein.
We have to swear you in first.
Please raise your right hand. Do you swear to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth before this committee and to respond honestly to Council Member questions? You may proceed.

Thank you, Chair, and thank you, Commissioner, for the opportunity to speak about what is a persistent concern about the persistent inequities we see in the impacted HIV on New Yorkers. As you noted, there’s been– in fact, it’s the fourth consecutive year that we’ve seen an uptick in new HIV diagnoses in the city, and we’re very concerned. We do, though, use the very robust information we capture in our HIV surveillance system to design an array of programs that are responsive to the epidemiologic trends and the– our knowledge of community’s needs related to HIV. And many of these are really aimed at supporting communities most affected. We know that we have to tailor our resources accordingly. So, the Commissioner mentioned our Play Sure Network 2.0 wherein we fund nearly 20 clinical and nonclinical agencies to provide an array of sexual health services including related to HIV,

really in a one-stop-shop model, and a whole person centered approach to give people all the services they need when they have that touchpoint with the health care system. And Play Sure providers are required to focus their efforts on serving communities most affected including Black and Latinx communities. Another good example of this programming is our Be Into Health program which is designed to support people living with HIV and really ensure that specifically members of these populations and communities we know are most disproportionately affected by HIV are achieving the HIV outcomes, that the tools and technologies exist to achieve, so that they are achieving viral suppression, that they are firmly engaged in high-quality HIV care so that their own health is protected and the public's health is protected. We certainly also have our sexual health clinics which provide really critical HIV and sexual health services, again, to communities we know aren’t able to or aren’t willing to access services elsewhere.

I appreciate that, and by the way, just mentioning the sexual health

clinics, my office also gets complaints about the one in Crown Heights that’s not there. So, particularly there was a need that was being filled there. So, we should really take a look at that. Why does DOHMH report new HIV diagnoses rather than estimated new infections as a PMMR metric?
Dr. Braunstein?

Sure. Thank you for that question. It’s a complex one, actually. But we– I mentioned our robust HIV surveillance system which we are very proud of how robust that system is and in that system we’re able to capture new HIV diagnoses which are based on laboratory and provider reports of positive HIV tests and new positive HIV tests. The metric that you mentioned, Chair Schulman, the estimated HIV incidents is really an estimate. It is based on a pretty complex model that CDC develops and that all Health Department jurisdictions use to estimate incident or new HIV infections. And so data on new HIV diagnoses which we can actually count and measure in our surveillance system are more reliable, more robust for tracking the epidemic here in New York City. So, that’s why

we report on new diagnoses in the PMMR, but we certainly do report on estimated incidents in our annual surveillance reports.
Okay. Given that the Trump administration has cut funding for HIV prevention programs, including access to PrEP, how is DOHMH planning to sustain HIV prevention and treatment services?

Yeah, thank you for that, Chair. We are closely monitoring the situation with regard to– bless you, Majority Leader– closely monitoring our exposure. As you know, $225 million in our budget goes to HIV and STI funding and 87 percent of that funding is exposed. And so we’re in constant conversations with OMB, with the Law Department and with the Mayor’s Office to shore up our defenses and make sure that we have a contingency plan in place. But I’ll hand it over to Aaron to see if he has more to add.

Yeah, just to add that over the last year we’ve watched– we’ve had this whiplash with the federal administration, right, around what’s going to happen.

There was a House proposal. There was the Senate proposal. There was the President’s budget. Each of them differed in the risk associated with what was going to happen with HIV funding. Ultimately, as it stands today, knock on wood, we’re in an okay place, but obviously, we remain vigilant always.

Access to sexual health prevention resources remains a critical component of the city’s HIV prevention strategy as new HIV diagnoses have increased in recent years. Nonprofit organizations reported in late 2024 that New York City’s Condom Availability Program which distributes free condoms through community partners was experiencing supply shortages. At the same time, recent clinic closures, including the Planned Parenthood of Greater New York Manhattan Health Center and two Brooklyn Sexual and Reproductive Health Centers operated by Public Health Solutions in Fort Greene and Brownsville raised concerns about access to testing, prevention resources, and sexual health services. Together these developments raised questions about whether New Yorkers have sufficient access to the prevention tools needed to reduce HIV

transmission. What is the current status of the reported condom shortage?
Thank you for that question, Chair. So, the NYCAP program or the Condom Access Program–
[interposing] Right.

is– our Condom Availability Program is one of the largest free safer sex programs in the country, and we take any disruptions in that supply seriously. We did experience a temporary supply shortage in 2024.
Okay.

We worked quickly with our vendors, with our distribution partners to make sure that we restored the inventory levels across our community partner network, and we have monitoring systems in place to make sure that we’re tracking distribution volume. We’re confident that our current supply can meet the demand.

Okay. That’s great. Given that the PMMR shows new HIV diagnoses have increased in the past two years, you know, does

DOHM believe that limited access to condoms or other prevention resources may have contributed to the trend?
